title: How to help children cope with stress, peer pressure: A brief guide to emotional well-being
content: How to help children cope with stress, peer pressure: A brief guide to emotional well-being Growing up isn't always smooth sailing. While your childhood and teenage years should be full of fun and discovery, it is completely natural to also experience heavy emotions like sadness, anger, anxiety, and stress. The most important thing to keep in mind is that you do not have to carry these feelings all on your own. You are surrounded by a secure network of parents, teachers, and friends who want to support you. Whenever things feel like they are getting a bit too much, there are simple, everyday strategies you can use to protect your peace of mind. What to do when you feel sad Just as it is natural to laugh when you are happy, it is completely normal and healthy to cry when you feel down. Crying is a natural physical release that helps ease the heavy weight in your heart. When you are feeling low, try talking to someone who is ready to listen—be it your parents, grandparents, or a school teacher you feel comfortable with. Writing down your thoughts in a diary can also help you categorise and process your feelings. If you feel trapped in your room, head outside for a brisk walk in the fresh air, or simply close your eyes and take a few slow, deep breaths. Managing sudden bursts of anger If you feel yourself starting to boil over with rage, the best first step is to remove yourself from the situation immediately. Pause and count slowly from one to ten in your mind. If you are in the middle of a heated argument, stop talking and take a slow sip of water. If you still feel a surge of restless, angry energy, try going for a quick run or doing a burst of physical exercise to burn it off safely. No matter how angry you get, make sure you never lash out or hurt anyone else—always choose constructive ways to let the feelings pass. What to do if you feel unsafe or mistreated If anyone ever behaves in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable, unsafe, or hurt, always remember that it is absolutely not your fault. You must report this immediately to your parents or a teacher you trust completely. Even if someone threatens you or commands you to keep it a secret, do not let fear silence you—always speak up to a trusted adult. You can also seek confidential, professional help by reaching out to the national child helpline on 1098. Resisting negative peer pressure Even if it is your best friend asking you to try something harmful, such as drugs or illicit substances, you must stand your ground and give a firm, clear "no". It is vital to report these incidents to your parents or school authorities immediately. Do not be intimidated if an older individual or someone you see every day pressures you; your safety must always come first. Similarly, look out for your friends. If you notice a classmate showing sudden changes in behaviour—such as extreme mood swings, constant drowsiness, chronic exhaustion, loss of appetite, or pulling away from social groups—gently share your concerns with a school teacher. For support with substance-use related challenges, the state-level Vimukthi helpline can be reached on 14405. Dealing with parental conflicts at home If your parents are arguing or shouting, try not to step in or get caught in the middle. Instead, wait for a quiet, calm moment later on to let them know how much their arguments upset and worry you. If ongoing family conflicts are starting to affect your studies or emotional health, do not keep it bottled up. Reach out and talk to your class teacher or the school counsellor. If you ever feel unsafe at home, help is always close at hand—dial 1098 or 112 for support. Building healthy daily habits Keeping your body active is a powerful way to lift your mood and clear your mind. Aim to play outdoors for at least 45 minutes every day after school. Simple habits like cycling, walking to nearby shops for errands, or opting for the stairs instead of the lift make a huge difference...
